(Update) John Sexton 9:20 PM | August 05, 2026 AP Photo/Pavel Bednyakov, Pool Something pretty strange happened today at an airport in Leipzig, Germany. An employee discovered an armed drone lying near a runway, not far from where some Ukrainian transport planes were located. A second drone reportedly hit a cargo plane taking off . Advertisement A drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the southern runway overnight into Wednesday. A second unidentified object collided with a cargo aircraft which had taken off later from the same airport. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover. There have been a series of unauthorised drone flights in Germany in recent months over sensitive sites including military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies... A police spokesman told the BBC that the object discovered overnight had been spotted close to parked Ukrainian Antonov transport planes. Because the first drone was intact, a bomb squad was called out and they x-rayed and defused it. The bomb it was carrying was not simply some fireworks. It contained Semtex . Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from the Ukraine war, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery... German media reported the attached bomb was made of PETN and semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty. A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”. Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in the Czech Republic, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around. Advertisement Officially, no one is saying what everyone is thinking, but this was not the work of some hack. It's being investigated as a possible political attack . The Dresden Public Prosecutor's Office and the Police Centre for Countering Terrorism and Extremism (PTAZ), based at the LKA, have taken charge of the investigation. Authorities have not ruled out a political motive, which is why the PTAZ is involved. This was likely another nation or a major league terrorist group. Why target this particular airport, possibly because it's a hub, for military supplies heading to Ukraine . Leipzig airport hosts the base of operations of NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution (SALIS), which gives participating countries access to Antonov cargo planes to transport military equipment. The airport is DHL’s largest European air hub and serves as an aircraft maintenance base for some Ukrainian Antonov aircraft. According to WELT, security authorities have internally classified the incident as an attempted attack. No suspects had been detained as of Wednesday evening. The other plane that was hit by something (probably another drone that didn't go off) belonged to DHS. After the strike, the plane was rerouted to Hanover where evidence of something hitting the nose was found. So what happened here? Well, we don't know but I'm going to speculate anyway. Russia has been taking a lot of drone hits lately on ships in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. It has also seen a bunch of Wildberries logistics hubs burn to the ground. The result has been a major disruption of Russia's economy. Advertisement It's not hard to believe that Putin would very much like to send a message to the Europeans supplying Ukraine with military support. However, a successful attack on a NATO country would be more heat than Putin can really handle. If you blow up a plane in Leipzig, no expense is going to be spared finding out who did it. And you run the risk of actually bringing NATO into a conflict you are already losing. However, you could send a warning, say an armed drone with a faulty detonator, or maybe two. You land one near a massive Ukrainian jet and you bonk the other into a plane at Europe's DHL hub. And the message seems pretty obvious: I can do to you what Ukraine is doing to me, scramble your shipping and economy with a few well-placed drones. In short, it looks like a threat. That's how Ukraine's ambassador to Germany sees it : The Ukrainian ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, suspects Russia is behind the drone incident. "I hope that all the authorities in Germany will now establish the facts. But who else could it be apart from Russia?" he told broadcaster Welt TV. Makeiev emphasized that Ukraine had gained a great deal of experience with drones during its war of defence against Russia. "Our experience is unique. And we are offering this expertise - from the military, our firefighters and our doctors - to our strategic partner, Germany." But if my speculation is right, it's an empty threat. There's a huge gap between showing you could do something and actually doing it. I think if Putin thought he could get away with crossing that line, he might do it. But it's a big risk. If he gets caught, that could be the end for him. Advertisement For now, I'd consider this a sign of growing desperation in the Kremlin. But who knows, maybe someone really meant for these bombs to go off in Germany. Update : Some new information. NEW: More details are emerging about yesterday's drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. According to WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, one of the Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft parked next to the drone was loaded with military ammunition that had recently arrived from France… pic.twitter.com/emrQWwkgUD — GeoInsider (@InsiderGeo) August 6, 2026 According to WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, one of the Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft parked next to the drone was loaded with military ammunition that had recently arrived from France and was awaiting onward transport, according to a confidential police report. Investigators say the drone was first seen hovering between two Antonov cargo aircraft before being forced to the ground by an airport employee, where authorities discovered the attached explosive device. Surveillance footage reportedly shows the drone entered the airport from the south at around 19:28, landed on the apron and remained there for several hours before being spotted shortly before midnight. According to Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, the drone was likely modified to evade existing counter-drone systems, which reportedly failed to detect it. Authorities are also investigating the second incident that occurred after the airport was temporarily closed. A DHL cargo aircraft was forced to abort its landing and reportedly collided with an unidentified object near the airport while traveling at approximately 500 km/h. Investigators believe the object may have been another drone. A bird strike has reportedly been deemed unlikely after forensic testing.
